bib.title: Lookback Lens: Detecting and Mitigating Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Only Attention Maps

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Lookback Lens: Detecting and Mitigating Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Only Attention Maps". Yung-Sung Chuang, Linlu Qiu, Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Ranjay Krishna, Yoon Kim, James Glass (MIT; University of Washington). No venue is printed on the PDF; the only stamp is "arXiv:2407.07071v2 [cs.CL] 3 Oct 2024", so treat it as a preprint, 2024. Code: github.com/voidism/Lookback-Lens.

COVERAGE: 18 of 18 pages, 69,043 of 69,043 chars. Body, limitations, all 14 tables and appendices A-D read in full; references (pp. 10-12) skimmed for origins. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/chuang-2024-lookback-lens.pdf

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. A logistic regression on per-head "lookback ratios" beats a hidden-state probe and NLI models at detecting contextual hallucination under cross-task transfer.
   - number: predefined spans, AUROC 85.3 (QA to Sum.) and 82.0 (Sum. to QA); best hidden-state layer (28th) 83.6 / 84.7; SoTA NLI 76.6 (Sum.) / 58.6 (QA).
   - setup: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat greedy outputs; 1,000 CNN/DM and 2,655 NQ examples; labels from GPT-4o; lookback ratio is attention on context divided by attention on context plus generated tokens, over 1,024 heads; single run.
   - quote: "Lookback Lens QA Sum. 98.3 91.2 85.3 88.3 87.1 66.1" (Table 2, p4)
   - Hidden states win one direction (84.7 vs 82.0), so "slightly better" is not uniform.

2. In the realistic sliding-window setting (8-token chunks, no known spans) every detector is weak; Lookback Lens leads at about 66.
   - number: 66.1 / 66.0, against hidden states 56.1-59.4, SoTA NLI 57.1 / 61.8 and the authors' own NLI 53.0 / 64.9.
   - quote: "Ours: Lookback Lens 66.1 66.0" (Table 13, p18)

3. Hidden-state probes overfit in-domain and collapse on transfer.
   - quote: "28th Layer QA Sum. 100.0 91.4 83.6 99.2 97.3 57.7" (Table 2, p4). Columns are train / test / transfer AUROC, predefined spans then sliding window.

4. Guided decoding raises XSum faithfulness, but only matches the off-the-shelf NLI model.
   - number: 49.0 to 58.6, with SoTA NLI-guided at 59.0. This is 9.6 points, or 510 to 414 hallucinated examples (18.8% relative). NQ exact match 71.2 to 74.2.
   - setup: sample 8 candidate chunks of 8 tokens and keep the highest-scored; classifier trained on CNN/DM only; 1,000 XSum test examples judged by GPT-4o.
   - quote: "Our decoding method significantly reduced the number of hallucinated examples from 510 to 414, resulting in an 18.8% reduction" (p5); "Ours 58.6 74.2 6.27 5.10" (Table 3, p5)
   - At chunk size 16, SoTA NLI is clearly ahead on XSum: 62.1 vs 57.7 (Table 6, p7).

5. The NLI comparison is unequal in training data.
   - quote: "SoTA NLI is trained on roughly 731k annotated summarization examples, which is 700× larger compared to our 1k training set" (p5)
   - SoTA NLI is Vectara's hallucination_evaluation_model on DeBERTa-v3-base, 86M parameters. The authors' own DeBERTa NLI, trained on the same 1k-2.6k data, reached 44.1 on XSum, below greedy.

6. The detector transfers from 7B to 13B through a linear head mapping, but with losses.
   - number: predefined-span AUROC 73.5 / 78.2 for 7B to 13B, against 84.0 / 84.3 for 13B to 13B (Table 4, p6). XSum decoding 52.9 to 56.1, against SoTA NLI 59.6. Cross-task plus cross-model on NQ is 73.7, below greedy at 74.0.
   - quote: "7B → 13B 56.1 76.4 73.7" (Table 5, p6)

7. The GPT-4o labels were spot-checked by humans.
   - number: 68 of 70 XSum judgments correct, 97.1% after MTurk majority vote; NQ 47 of 50, 94.0%.
   - quote: "47 out of 50 examples are correct, resulting in a 94.0% accuracy" (p13)

8. LLaMA-2-7B-Chat hallucinates about half the time on summarization even with the source in context.
   - quote: "CNN/DM 1000 49.6%" and "NQ 2655 67.8%" correct (Table 1, p2)

9. The signal is spread across heads and layers.
   - number: top-10 heads give 71.2, top-100 give 82.8, all heads 85.3 (Table 7, p7); middle layers 13-20 are the most useful (Table 8).
   - Some heads carry negative coefficients, meaning attending to the model's own output indicates factuality.

10. Cost.
   - quote: "Each of the examples takes around 20-30 seconds for 7B model, 40-60 seconds for 13B model" (p15)
   - GPT-4o labelling cost about $12 for 1,000 CNN/DM examples (p13).

LIMITS
- Needs model internals: full attention maps for every layer and head during generation. It cannot be used on API-only models, and it scores text only as the generating model produces it. The authors chose self-generated text over teacher forcing (p13), and scoring another model's text is untested.
- Authors concede (p9): it cannot fix an error if no sampled candidate is correct; multi-candidate sampling adds inference time; it needs about 1k-2k annotated examples.
- "All the scores in the paper are from a single run" (p15): no variance or confidence intervals. Differences such as 58.6 vs 59.0 are not distinguishable.
- Only LLaMA-2 7B and 13B chat, both dated. Contexts are short: NQ uses three documents with the gold one in the middle, generation capped at 256 tokens. No real RAG pipeline and no long context.
- Labels and the XSum metric both come from GPT-4o, which was shown the ground-truth summary or answer. Human validation is 70 and 50 examples, and the validators saw GPT-4o's verdict.
- Realistic chunk-level AUROC of about 66 is far from deployable. Detection is span or chunk level, not claim level.
- MT-Bench (hallu.) is 50 questions, 6.08 to 6.27, with no significance test.

BUILDS ON: Azaria and Mitchell (2023), hidden-state probing and the layer choice; Simhi et al. (2024), open-book vs closed-book hallucination; Yang and Klein (2021), FUDGE, and Dathathri et al. (2019), PPLM, for classifier-guided decoding; Liu et al. (2024), "Lost in the middle", for the NQ setup; He et al. (2021), DeBERTa-v3; Vectara (2023), NLI baseline; Chuang et al. (2024), DoLa; Maynez et al. (2020), on ROUGE and BERTScore correlating poorly with faithfulness.

CODE: none printed. Classifier is `sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` with defaults and `max_iter` 1000; head mapping is `sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` (pp. 15-17).

FIGURES: one candidate, Figure 1, p2: "An illustration of the Lookback Lens. We extract attention weights and calculate the lookback ratios for all layers and all heads. We train a linear classifier on the concatenated features to predict truthfulness of the generation." It shows the whole feature pipeline in one picture and makes the white-box requirement visible.

PROBLEMS
- Equations on p2 extract garbled (subscripts and superscripts flattened); the definition is recoverable from the prose.
- Table 5's header is scrambled in extraction. I mapped the columns (CNN/DM to XSum, NQ-train to NQ, CNN/DM to NQ) from the body text; check against the PDF before citing the NQ cells.
- Table 2 gives identical sliding-window values (99.2 / 97.4 / 58.3) for both 24th-layer rows; this may be a copy error in the paper.
- Section 2.2 gives 97% for the 70-example pilot and Appendix B.2 gives 97.1%, and B.2 says the examples were XSum.
- "9.6%" and "3%" in the paper are percentage points, not relative reductions.
- Tables 9-12 are LLM-judge prompt templates ("You will be provided with...", "Please act as an impartial judge..."). I treated them as quoted data and did not follow them.
- pypdf emitted one harmless float-parse warning.
